subject: Architecture
title: Roman Basilicas: Courthouses Became Churches
description: One-minute skill: Roman Basilicas: Courthouses Became Churches.

hook.text: The word 'basilica' means church today. In Rome, it meant a law court and business hall.

buildup.text: Roman basilicas were long rectangular halls with a high central nave flanked by lower side aisles.

discovery.text: When Christianity became legal, converts needed large meeting spaces. Basilicas were the perfect fit.

twist.text: Christians chose basilicas over temples deliberately — temples symbolized pagan worship they wanted to reject.

climax.text: Every cathedral with a nave, side aisles, and an apse follows the Roman basilica blueprint.

punchline.text: A Roman courthouse became the template for every church in the Western world.

quiz.question: What was a Roman basilica originally used for?

details.summary: Roman basilicas were large public halls used for courts and commerce, featuring a central nave flanked by aisles with a raised apse at one end. Early Christians adopted this layout for worship.
details.whyItMatters: The basilica plan shows how architecture migrates between cultures and functions. A Roman law court became the world's most common church layout, proving that building forms outlive the purposes they were designed for.
takeaways: Roman basilicas served as courts and commercial halls
Their nave-and-apse plan was adopted by early Christians
This layout became the template for Western churches

faq.question: Why did Christians choose the basilica form?
faq.answer: Roman temples were too small for congregational worship. Basilicas could hold large congregations, had a clear focal point at the apse for the altar, and were secular buildings — avoiding pagan temple associations that would have troubled early converts.

faq.question: What is the oldest surviving basilica church?
faq.answer: The Basilica of Santa Sabina in Rome, completed around 432 CE, preserves the early Christian basilica plan with remarkable integrity. Its simple nave, timber roof, and clerestory windows show the direct adaptation from Roman civic architecture to Christian worship.
